courses.title: Introduction to Computers
courses.summary: Learn what a computer is, how its parts work together, and how to use one with confidence.

description.text: This short course is for anyone who has never used a computer, or who uses one but does not feel sure about it. It uses plain language and everyday examples, with no technical background needed.
You can read the lessons at your own pace. Each lesson takes about five to ten minutes.

outcomes: Name the main parts of a computer and what each one does
Start, use and shut down a computer safely
courses.audience: Complete beginners of any age, including students and adults returning to study.

sections.title: Getting to know the computer
sections.summary: The parts and what they do.

lessons.title: What is a computer?
lessons.summary: A computer takes in information, processes it and gives a result.

body.text: A computer is a machine that follows instructions. You give it information (input), it works on that information (processing), it may keep it (storage), and it shows you a result (output).
Everyday examples

items: Typing a message on a phone: your fingers are the input, the screen is the output.
Searching for a word on the internet: the computer processes your request and returns pages.
Saving a photo: the computer stores it so you can open it later.

body.text: Phones, tablets and laptops are all computers. They differ in size and how you control them, not in what they do.

lessons.title: Hardware and software
lessons.summary: Hardware is what you can touch. Software is the instructions that make it useful.

body.text: Hardware is every physical part of a computer: the screen, keyboard, mouse and the parts inside. Software is the set of programs that tell the hardware what to do.
Common hardware

items: Monitor or screen: shows what the computer is doing
Keyboard and mouse: let you give instructions
Processor (CPU): does the calculations
Memory (RAM): holds what you are working on right now
Storage (hard disk or SSD): keeps your files when the computer is off

body.text: Common software

items: Operating system, such as Windows, Android or macOS: manages the computer
Applications, such as a web browser or a word processor: help you do tasks

sections.title: Using a computer
sections.summary: Starting up, files and staying safe.

lessons.title: Starting up and shutting down
lessons.summary: Turn a computer on and off the right way to protect your work.

body.text: Press the power button once and wait for the sign-in screen. Enter your password if asked. Avoid pressing buttons repeatedly while it loads.
To shut down properly

items: Save your work and close your programs
Open the Start menu or the power menu
Choose Shut down and wait for the screen to go dark

body.text: Holding the power button to switch off should be a last resort. It can damage files that were still being saved.

lessons.title: Files and folders
lessons.summary: Keep your documents organised so you can always find them.

body.text: A file is one item you save, such as a document, photo or song. A folder is a container that groups files, like a paper folder in a cabinet.
Habits that help

items: Give files clear names, such as Cv-Amina-2026 instead of Document1
Keep related files in one folder
Back up important files on a second device or a trusted online drive

courses.title: Internet and Email
courses.summary: Search the web safely, create an email account and write a professional message.

description.text: Learn how the internet works at a basic level, how to find reliable information, and how to use email for school, work and applications.

outcomes: Explain what the internet and a web browser are
Search effectively and judge whether a website can be trusted
courses.audience: Learners who can use a computer or phone and want to use the internet confidently.

lessons.title: How the internet works
lessons.summary: The internet is a worldwide network of connected computers.

body.text: The internet connects billions of computers so they can share information. When you open a website, your device asks another computer, called a server, to send you the page.

items: A web browser, such as Chrome or Firefox, is the program you use to view websites
A web address, such as example.com, tells the browser which server to ask
Wi-Fi or mobile data connects your device to the internet

lessons.title: Searching and trusting sources
lessons.summary: Find good answers and spot unreliable pages.

body.text: Type a few specific words into a search engine rather than a long sentence. Try different words if the first search does not help.
Questions to ask about a website

items: Who wrote it, and can you find their name or organisation?
When was it written or updated?
Do other trusted sources say the same thing?
Is it trying to sell you something or make you feel rushed?

body.text: A page that looks professional is not automatically true. Compare at least two sources for anything important.

lessons.title: Creating an email account
lessons.summary: Choose a professional address and protect your account.

body.text: An email address is like a postal address for messages. Many services offer free accounts.
Choosing an address

items: Use your real name, for example amina.uwase
Avoid nicknames or numbers that look unprofessional when applying for jobs or internships

body.text: Protecting it

items: Use a long password that you do not use anywhere else
Turn on two-step verification if the service offers it
Never share your password, even with someone who says they are from the service

lessons.title: Writing a professional email
lessons.summary: Clear subject, short message, polite ending.

body.text: A good email is easy to read in thirty seconds.

items: Subject: say what the email is about, for example Internship application: Amina Uwase
Greeting: Dear Mr Habimana, or Hello Ms Uwase,
Body: one request per email, in short paragraphs
Closing: thank the reader and add your full name and phone number

body.text: Attachments
Mention the attachment in your message and give it a clear name, such as Amina-Uwase-CV.pdf.

lessons.title: Recognising online scams
lessons.summary: Most scams try to rush you or ask for secrets.

body.text: Scammers pretend to be a bank, a mobile money service, an employer or a friend. They want your money or your passwords.
Warning signs

items: A message says you won a prize you never entered
Someone asks for your PIN, password or a verification code
You are told to act immediately or lose your account
The sender asks you to pay a fee to receive a job or an internship

body.text: Real organisations never ask for your PIN or password. If in doubt, stop and contact them using a phone number you already trust.
